source: Mercado (2016) Commentary: Interpretations without justification: a general argument against Morgan's Canon
finding: Philosophers (Fitzpatrick 2008, Heyes 2012, Buckner 2013, Starzak 2016) argue Morgan's Canon has no sound basis for choosing between explanations. 'Lower' is read in many ways: simpler, implicit, reflexive, or phylogenetically older. Starzak says prefer the explanation with more evidence. Mercado adds that animal data rarely favour one explanation, so the jury is deadlocked.
numbers: No data. Morgan (1903, p.59) is quoted.
quote: In no case is an animal activity to be interpreted in terms of higher psychological processes, if it can be fairly interpreted in terms of processes which stand lower
limits: A commentary, not an experiment. Mercado says it is hard to tell whether the Canon helped or hurt progress, and that it may bias researchers toward under-attributing cognition.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code 'pick the simplest mechanism' in the schema. Pick the explanation with more evidence and say what the evidence is (G3).

source: Starzak (2016) as described in Mercado (2016): drop Morgan's Canon for general scientific principles
finding: Claimed justifications for the Canon (digs deeper, protects from error, checks anthropomorphism, promotes test-validity checks; Karin-D'Arcy 2005) lack evidence. Philosophers who examined them found them weak or invalid.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand: seen only through Mercado's summary. Original Starzak paper not read.
agent_relevance: Any rule that says 'prefer the simple story' needs its own test. We can measure whether it lowers false claims in our agent.

source: Kano, Krupenye, Hirata, Tomasello, Call (2017) A test of the submentalizing hypothesis: Apes' performance in a false belief task inanimate control
finding: Heyes proposed the apes' anticipatory looks came from low-level cueing (the actor's green shirt as a retrieval cue). Test: replace the human and the gorilla actor with a green half-circle and a grey triangle. Apes tracked the events but anticipated much less and showed no tendency to look to the correct box. The simple rival did not match the data.
numbers: N=43 apes in control. 22/43 (51.16%) made an anticipatory look vs 22/30 (73.33%) in the original. Of 22 looks, 14 went first to the Target (p=0.28, binomial). FB1: 6/11 (p=1.0). FB2: 8/11 (p=0.23).
limits: The rival made a clear prediction and the data went against it. The control is not perfectly matched, and a null on the control is not proof of mentalizing. Rival may need other controls.
agent_relevance: Template for a parsimony test that discriminates: keep the low-level cue, strip the mind-relevant structure, see whether the effect survives. For the agent: stripped or mutated inputs (G3).

source: Kano, Krupenye, Hirata, Call, Tomasello (2017) Eye tracking uncovered great apes' ability to anticipate that other individuals will act according to false beliefs (methods account)
finding: Explains why apes passed an anticipatory-looking false-belief test when earlier tests failed. Three differences: eye movements as the measure, a design adapted from a human-infant test, and scenes built to hold ape attention. Past failures may reflect task demands, not missing ability.
numbers: No new data. The original (Krupenye et al. 2016 Science) had 22 of 30 apes make an anticipatory look, per the control paper.
limits: Only the abstract and opening were read. This is the authors' own account of their design, not independent confirmation.
agent_relevance: Failure under one test format is weak evidence of absence. Same lesson as Hu and Frank: change the format before concluding a model lacks a skill.

source: Kampis, Kovacs, Csibra, Southgate, Hernik et al. (2021) A two-lab direct replication attempt of Southgate, Senju and Csibra (2007)
finding: Preregistered replication of the infant anticipatory-looking false-belief study, with two original authors involved. No evidence of action anticipation. Only about half the infants looked to the agent's impending action, even when no belief tracking was needed. The paradigm does not reliably elicit action prediction, so it cannot test false-belief understanding at age 2.
numbers: 160 infants aged 24-26 months, two sites. 70 excluded, 90 left. 49/90 (54%) anticipated correctly at the second familiarisation trial (original 20/31, 65%). 22/49 anticipated correctly at test, p=0.568 vs chance.
limits: Does not show infants lack theory of mind; it shows this measure fails. Authors cite other non-replications (Burnside et al. 2018; Duhn and Rakoczy 2018).
agent_relevance: A method can be widely cited and still fail replication. Treat any single-task pass as a pointer, not proof.

source: Kulke and Rakoczy (2019) Why can some implicit Theory of Mind tasks be replicated and others cannot? A test of mentalizing versus submentalizing explanations
finding: Three preregistered experiments tested whether the replicable and non-replicable anticipatory-looking conditions differ because the replicable ones can be solved by submentalizing. Result: no unambiguous evidence for reliable spontaneous ToM, no effect of number of passed familiarisation trials, and the submentalizing account did not explain the mixed pattern either.
numbers: First saccades: FB1 7/12 to the belief-congruent side (58%, p=.774, BF10=0.643). FB2 5/7 (71%, p=.453, BF10=0.965). TB1 9/16 (56%, p=.804, BF10=0.571). Many made no look at all (13, 18, 9 participants).
limits: Small usable samples after exclusions. Bayes factors near 1 mean the data favour neither account. Authors call the picture puzzling.
agent_relevance: The simple rival does not always win. When both accounts fit poorly, say 'unresolved' rather than forcing the cheaper story.

source: Conway, Lee, Ojaghi, Catmur, Bird (2017) Submentalizing or mentalizing in a Level 1 perspective-taking task: A cloak and goggles test
finding: In the dot-perspective task, an avatar's view slows the person's dot count. Santiesteban et al. found the same effect with an arrow, so mentalizing was doubted. This study added an invisibility cloak and opaque and transparent goggles so that mentalizing and domain-general attention predict different results. No evidence of automatic mentalizing was found. Empathy and perspective-taking scores did not predict performance, contradicting earlier work.
numbers: Experiment 1 (cloak) found no mentalizing signature. Two further 'well-powered' goggles experiments (as stated in the abstract) also found none. Exact N not extracted.
limits: Supports the simple account for this task only. Exact samples not read.
agent_relevance: Here the cheap account won, after a design that could have shown otherwise. The key was a condition where the two accounts make opposite predictions.

source: Schmidjell, Range, Huber, Viranyi (2012) Do owners have a Clever Hans effect on dogs? Results of a pointing study
finding: Direct test of an owner-cue (Clever Hans) explanation of dogs following pointing. Whether the owner was blind, informed of the right box, or told the wrong box did not change dogs' choices. With no pointing, dogs chose at chance even when owners knew where the reward was. When owners were told to steer actively they did succeed, but less if the experimenter had pointed elsewhere.
numbers: Exp 1: 69 dogs analysed (of 75 pairs). Above chance with pointing in all three groups (Blindfolded N=17 p=0.003; Enhancement N=18 p=0.002; Decrease N=17 p=0.003). No pointing N=17 at chance (p=0.839). Exp 2: Owner active N=16 p=0.001; Pointing + Owner active N=15 p=0.059.
limits: Owners sat behind dogs and were told not to cue. Undetected cues cannot be fully excluded. Individually, only 3 dogs per pointing group were above chance.
agent_relevance: The Clever Hans test is cheap: vary what the person who knows the answer knows. For the agent: vary what the checker or prompt reveals about the answer and see if performance moves.

source: Samhita and Gross (2013) The 'Clever Hans Phenomenon' revisited
finding: Retells Pfungst's 1907 investigation: Hans solved tasks by reading tiny face and posture signals of the questioner and audience. After this, experimenters avoided face-to-face contact; the authors say this lesson is still not applied rigorously.
numbers: No new numbers in the text read.
limits: Short essay. Pfungst's exact scores were not in the text read.
agent_relevance: The original parsimony win was a blinding test. Our version: hide the answer from every component that could leak it.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Kosinski claimed GPT-3.5 passes classic false-belief tasks. Ullman made small changes that keep the ToM logic the same (transparent bag, a label Sam cannot read, a trusted friend's warning, a protagonist who put the item there himself). Answers did not flip as they should: the model still said Sam believes the bag holds chocolate. He says the simplest account is that the model has not learned ToM, and that outlying failures should count for more than average success.
numbers: Transparent bag: P(chocolate)=95% for Sam's belief. Trusted friend said 'ignore the label': P(chocolate)=97%. Cat in the box, Mark put it there: P(basket)=54% vs P(box)=43%.
quote: we should not place the two possibilities on equal footing, but start by presuming strongly that they have not
limits: Single author, one GPT-3.5-era model, a handful of vignettes, token probabilities not sample statistics. Version 5 corrects an error: a double space caused a false flip on one prompt (latest model: P(chocolate) 53%, P(popcorn) 39%).
agent_relevance: Perturbation tests (G3) should be standard. A gap between average and worst case is the signal.

source: Ullman (2023), discussion: benchmarks, contamination and the future of the Kosinski dilemma
finding: Warning: once a perturbation generator or benchmark is published, a model can train on it and pass without learning the skill. Even if a later model passes all variants, one can still doubt ToM because people infer mental states from process, not only behaviour (a recorded 'have a nice day' is not the same as a person saying it).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument by the author, not tested.
agent_relevance: Rotate and hide held-out perturbations. A pass on a public benchmark is weaker than a pass on a fresh mutation (G3, contamination tests).

source: Shapira, Levy, Alavi, Zhou, Choi, Goldberg, Sap, Shwartz (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind? Stress Testing Social Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Six ToM tasks. Models show some ToM-like behaviour but it is not robust. On adversarial variants (Adv-CSFB) performance collapses, fitting shallow heuristics. Probing method changes scores. The authors say 40 examples (Kosinski) or 10 (Bubeck) are too few to claim emergence.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on ToMi: 81% overall but 46% on false-belief questions. GPT-4 on SocialIQa: 79% total, 61% on 'others' effects. GPT-4 on FauxPas-EAI: 27%, below the most-frequent-class baseline. flan-t5-xxl on TriangleCOPA: 96%. Adversarial categories, davinci-002 to GPT-4: 'inon' 71.4% to 0%; transparent access 66.7% to 0%; other person 93.8% to 68.8%. GPT-4 on original false-belief items: 97%.
quote: LLMs rely on shortcuts, heuristics, and spurious correlations
limits: Probing method matters (7-point gap for GPT-4 on SocialIQa between multiple-choice and chain-of-thought). Adversarial items written by one author and checked by another. Reporting bias in training text offered as one cause.
agent_relevance: Newer, more helpful models did worse on some adversarial items. More capability does not mean more robustness. Track the worst-category score, not just the mean.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks, PNAS
finding: Eleven LLMs on 40 hand-made false-belief tasks; each task has a false-belief scenario, three true-belief controls and reversed versions, and a model must get all eight prompts right. Older models solved none. davinci-002 solved 5%, davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo 20%, ChatGPT-4 75%, level with six-year-old children. Author suggests ToM-like ability may be a by-product of language skill.
numbers: ChatGPT-4: 75% of tasks, 95% CI [66%, 84%]; 90% on unexpected-contents tasks. Correlation between task types R=0.98 (CI 0.92-0.99).
limits: Only 40 hand-made tasks that may resemble training text. Ullman and Shapira later broke earlier models with small perturbations.
agent_relevance: This is the claim the parsimony camp tests. It sets the baseline: strong average score, doubtful robustness.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Battery of ToM measures (false belief, indirect requests, irony, faux pas, misdirection) given repeatedly to GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2 and compared with 1,907 people. GPT-4 matched or beat humans on indirect requests, false beliefs and misdirection but struggled on faux pas. LLaMA2 beat humans on faux pas, but a belief-likelihood follow-up showed this was a bias toward attributing ignorance.
numbers: Humans N=1,907 overall. Belief-likelihood follow-up: 900 humans, 270 observations per model. False-belief perturbations: 757 humans, 225 observations per model.
limits: Wording and scoring change conclusions. Output is 'consistent with' mentalistic inference, which is not proof of the mechanism.
agent_relevance: A rival-hypothesis step (rewording to likelihood) changed the verdict on two models. Use paired wordings (G3).

source: Strachan et al. (2024), faux pas follow-up on why GPT failed
finding: GPT's faux-pas failure looked like inability. Rewording from a yes/no question to a likelihood question ('is it more likely that X remembered or did not remember') suggested the failure was hyperconservatism, not failed inference.
numbers: Follow-up used three variants per item (faux pas, neutral, knowledge-implied), 15 repetitions per item per ChatGPT model, each in a separate chat session.
quote: the poor performance of GPT originated from a hyperconservative approach towards committing to conclusions
limits: Exact score changes not extracted. The interpretation is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Failures can come from output-format caution, not lack of skill. Do not read refusal-to-commit as a reasoning error.

source: Authors D.K.F.P., S.K.Y.P., M.D.B., A.H. (2025) Do large language models have a theory of mind? (letter), PNAS
finding: Applies the comparative-cognition toolkit to LLMs. Morgan's Canon may lack justification, but 'association-blindness' is also a mistake. Rival explanations: associative learning, explicit training on ToM-like items, pattern matching. Proposes a goggles-style test: say the container is transparent; wrongly inferring a false belief would point to trained pattern-matching. Calls for converging evidence, not isolated tasks.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: attributing ToM to LLMs may be premature until simpler explanations can be ruled out
limits: A short untested letter. Notes the sudden jump in newer models is consistent with explicit training.
agent_relevance: Direct bridge to our agent: transparent-container check, and tasks with radically different patterns. Warns against both over- and under-attribution.

source: Sap, Le Bras, Fried, Choi (2022) Neural Theory-of-Mind? On the Limits of Social Intelligence in Large LMs
finding: Early test of GPT-3 on SocialIQa and ToMi. Weak results, and an argument from pragmatics that next-word training alone is unlikely to give ToM. More shots helped little.
numbers: GPT-3 about 55% on SocialIQa and 60% on ToMi, well below human. Raising few-shot examples from 10 to 35 on SocialIQa gave about 1 point.
limits: 2022 models. Later models did far better on the same sets, so this failure verdict aged fast.
agent_relevance: Re-run old failure results on the current model before using them as a design constraint.

source: Hu and Frank (2024) Auxiliary task demands mask the capabilities of smaller language models, COLM
finding: Borrows 'task demands' from child psychology. In analogical reasoning, reflective reasoning, word prediction and grammaticality judgement, high-demand formats (verbal or metalinguistic output) gave lower scores than low-demand formats (forced choice or direct probability). The gap is biggest for smaller models and shrinks with size.
numbers: Demand gap = log-odds difference (forced choice minus production). Pythia, OLMo, Gemma, Llama-2, Mistral, 1B to 70B parameters. Trend is a decrease with size; exact gaps are in figures. In grammaticality, Pythia and OLMo stayed near 50% chance under the metalinguistic method.
limits: Which format is the 'right' measure is not settled. Values here are trends, not extracted figures.
agent_relevance: The opposite parsimony error: under-attribution. Check a low-demand format before declaring a failure.

source: McCoy, Yao, Friedman, Hardy, Griffiths (2023) Embers of Autoregression: Understanding Large Language Models Through the Problem They are Trained to Solve
finding: A mechanism-based simple explanation for LLM errors. Because models are shaped by next-word prediction, they do better when the task, the output or the input is high-probability, even when the task is deterministic. Eleven tasks on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4: cipher decoding 51% with high-probability output vs 13% with low. Reverse a word sequence 97% vs 53%. Pig Latin 42% (common variant) vs 23% (rare). Rot-13 encoding 21% (high-prob input) vs 11% (low). Shift ciphers: 50% or more only for shifts 1, 3, 13; below 3% for the rest.
limits: Two models only. A probability account is one more candidate explanation, not a refutation of reasoning.
agent_relevance: A rival, testable low-level account. Test: put an improbable but valid answer in and see if accuracy falls.

source: Wu, Qiu, Ross, Akyurek, Chen, Wang, Kim, Andreas, Kim (2023) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Eleven task pairs (default vs counterfactual rule, such as base-9 instead of base-10 addition, 1-based indexing, altered chess rules, drop-D tuning). Models show non-trivial counterfactual ability, but performance drops from the default, suggesting part of the success rests on default-specific behaviour rather than abstract reasoning. Frequency of the default variant matters.
numbers: Eleven tasks. Exact default vs counterfactual accuracies are in figures and were not extracted.
quote: success of existing LMs on standard benchmarks should not be considered as sufficient evidence for their possession of full general capacity
limits: Counterfactual accuracy stayed above chance on most tasks, so this is partial memorisation, not zero reasoning. Chain-of-thought helps unevenly.
agent_relevance: The best fit for our G3 mutated-input idea. Report the default-vs-counterfactual gap as a contamination measure per task.

source: Gu, Tafjord, Kim, Moore, Le Bras, Clark, Choi (2026) SimpleToM: Exposing the Gap Between Explicit ToM Inference and Implicit ToM Application in LLMs, ICLR 2026
finding: Everyday stories with hidden information. Three questions each: awareness (explicit), behaviour prediction, behaviour judgement (applied). Strong models infer the mental state but fail to apply it; judgement falls far below chance.
numbers: Mental state: over 95% for Llama-3.1-405B, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o. Behaviour prediction: GPT-3.5 7.6%, small models under 40%. Judgement for the large models 10% to 24.9%; best (DeepSeek-R1) 65.8%.
limits: Binary questions (chance 50%), 95% CIs reported. Below-chance scores mean a systematic wrong preference, not noise.
agent_relevance: Ask for the inference and the action that should follow from it. Passing the first and failing the second means the skill is not usable.

source: Gu et al. (2026), SimpleToM interventions
finding: Test-time fixes did not close the gap. Chain-of-thought left every model under 40% on behaviour judgement. A reminder to consider the character's mental state raised behaviour prediction above 80% for the models, but judgement stayed low for some. The paper concludes no simple test-time intervention reliably patches applied ToM.
numbers: With the reminder, GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-405B reached only 42.2% and 25.8% on behaviour judgement. One case: Claude-3.5-Sonnet judgement went from 24.9% to 84.1%.
limits: Numbers differ by model and question type; only the ones above were checked.
agent_relevance: A specific cue to apply the mental state works better than a generic 'think step by step'. A G2-style cue from real output.

source: Kim, Sclar, Zhou, Le Bras, Kim, Choi, Sap (2023) FANToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
finding: Conversations where a character leaves and misses information. The same reasoning is asked in several question forms, so a lucky pass on one form is caught by another. Models are far below humans even with chain-of-thought or fine-tuning.
numbers: Strictest score: humans 87.5; GPT-4 0613 + CoT 26.6 (June) or 14.8 (October); ChatGPT 3.7; Llama-2-Chat 0.4; Mistral 0.1; fine-tuned Flan-T5 XL 53.7. Answerability list+Y/N: humans 90.6, GPT-4 40.2.
limits: Requiring all question forms right is harsh. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Consistency across paraphrased questions on one fact is a cheap detector of illusory competence (G3).

source: Survey of practitioners (2025) Morgan's canon and the associative-cognitive distinction today, Journal of Comparative Psychology
finding: Found in a Europe PMC listing only. Title says comparative psychologists were surveyed on how they use the Canon and the associative-versus-cognitive split today.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Not opened. Content unknown beyond the title.
agent_relevance: Worth opening later to see how much the field still uses the Canon.

source: Heyes (2012) Simple minds: a qualified defence of associative learning, Phil Trans R Soc B
finding: Cited by Mercado as a source that qualifies Morgan's Canon and contrasts associative with more sophisticated explanations. Full text not available through the tool used.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Not opened. Only what Mercado's commentary attributes to it.
agent_relevance: Main source for 'associative does not mean simple' and for submentalizing (see b03).

source: Heyes (2014) Submentalizing: I Am Not Really Reading Your Mind, Perspectives on Psychological Science
finding: As described by Kano et al. (2017): submentalizing is prediction of behaviour by low-level, domain-general processes. Heyes suggested inanimate controls to test it, such as treating the green shirt as a retrieval cue in Krupenye et al.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Second-hand through Kano et al. 2017.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean way to state a rival: name the low-level cue, build a control that keeps it, predict what the rival says.

source: Shettleworth (2010) Clever animals and killjoy explanations in comparative psychology, Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: Found in a Europe PMC listing (122 citations) and cited by Mercado for treating widespread (phylogenetically older) capacities as 'lower'. Full text not read.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Not opened. Only the title and Mercado's description.
agent_relevance: Killjoy explanations can be right or wrong, and each needs its own test, same as the flashy one.

source: Anonymous author (2026) Zombies without puppeteers: Morgan's Canon and the passive manipulation hypothesis in Xenos vesparum, Frontiers in Parasitology
finding: Applies Morgan's Canon to a parasite-host system. Proposes passive activation of existing host responses as the null model: parasite-benefiting behaviour alone does not prove parasite-designed control. Calls for comparing true infection, mechanical insult, parasite secretions and natural alternative phenotypes.
numbers: Archived pilot: a sterile nylon implant (no signalling) was linked to lower energy use and nest desertion in Polistes dominula workers; encapsulation intensity did not predict metabolic change. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Perspective piece with a small pilot; the author says it does not prove passive manipulation. Not an LLM study.
agent_relevance: Same rule outside primates: the right control is a mechanical stand-in with no agency that still triggers the response (the nylon thread is the inanimate control).
